questions.q: Why can reporting the best Sharpe ratio out of many tested strategy variations be misleading?
options: Because Sharpe ratios cannot be compared across strategies
Because even if every variation had zero true skill, pure randomness guarantees some will show an impressively high Sharpe ratio by chance, and only the winner gets reported
Because Sharpe ratios are only valid for a single asset
Because the best strategy is always overfit by definition
questions.explain: This is multiple-testing (selection) bias: testing many variations and reporting only the best result ignores that some high Sharpe ratios will appear purely by chance when many trials are run, even with zero true skill.

questions.q: What does the Probabilistic Sharpe Ratio (PSR) adjust for that a raw Sharpe ratio does not?
options: The number of assets in the portfolio
Sample size and the return distribution's skewness and kurtosis
The number of trading days per year
The correlation between strategies
questions.explain: PSR computes the probability that the true Sharpe ratio exceeds a benchmark, accounting for how many return observations there are and for skewness/kurtosis in the return distribution, since Sharpe ratio estimates from short or non-normal samples are less reliable.

questions.q: What benchmark does the Deflated Sharpe Ratio (DSR) test the observed Sharpe ratio against, instead of zero?
options: The risk-free rate
The expected maximum Sharpe ratio that would arise from N zero-skill trials, given the number of trials and their dispersion
The Sharpe ratio of a buy-and-hold benchmark index
The average Sharpe ratio of all mutual funds
questions.explain: DSR evaluates the Probabilistic Sharpe Ratio against a benchmark equal to the expected maximum Sharpe ratio you'd observe from N trials under zero true skill — a benchmark that rises with the number of trials and how much their Sharpe ratios vary.

questions.q: Is the Deflated Sharpe Ratio available as a built-in scikit-learn function?
options: Yes, sklearn.metrics.deflated_sharpe_ratio
Yes, but only in the development/nightly build of scikit-learn
No — it combines several statistical pieces and is typically hand-implemented or obtained from a specialized research library
No, and it cannot be implemented without proprietary data
questions.explain: DSR is not an sklearn function. It combines the probabilistic Sharpe ratio (adjusted for skewness/kurtosis/sample size) with an expected-maximum-Sharpe-ratio benchmark derived from the number of trials, and is typically coded by hand or sourced from a specialized quant research package.

questions.q: What does a Deflated Sharpe Ratio near 0.5 suggest about a strategy's headline Sharpe ratio?
options: The strategy is guaranteed to be profitable going forward
The headline Sharpe ratio is exactly what you'd expect from pure multiple-testing luck, not necessarily genuine skill
The strategy has a Sharpe ratio of exactly 0.5 after rounding
The strategy should be deployed immediately with maximum leverage
questions.explain: A DSR near 0.5 (or below) indicates the observed Sharpe ratio is about what would be expected from pure luck across the number of trials attempted, not strong evidence of genuine skill.
